notes.meaning: Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests began the work by rebuilding the Sheep Gate. This gate stood near the temple, and sheep meant for animal sacrifices were brought through it. The priests dedicated this gate and their stretch of wall to place the whole project under God's protection. Spiritual leaders set a good example when they are the first to step forward in hard work.

Men from the nearby town of Jericho built the next section of wall, alongside a man named Zaccur. People from outside Jerusalem came to help even though they did not live within the city itself. Their willingness shows how believers from different places pulled together to protect the house of God.

A family clan called the sons of Hassenaah rebuilt the Fish Gate on the north wall. They set up the timber beams, hung the heavy doors, and fitted the metal bolts and bars to secure it. This gate likely got its name from the market where fishermen brought their catch into the city.

Three leaders named Meremoth, Meshullam, and Zadok repaired the next three stretches of the wall. The word used for repair means they strengthened and patched up the broken places. Each man took charge of his assigned part so that the work moved forward without delay.

The ordinary people of Tekoa worked on the next section, but their nobles refused to help. These wealthy leaders thought physical labor was beneath their rank and would not submit to the work of the Lord. When rulers hold back, humble believers often step up and do the work anyway.

Two men, Joiada and Meshullam, repaired the Jeshanah Gate, often known as the Old Gate. They laid its wooden roof beams and installed its doors, locks, and metal bars. Working as partners allowed them to finish a large project that one person could not easily manage alone.

Melatiah from Gibeon, Jadon from Meronoth, and men from Mizpah repaired the next section. These towns lay outside Jerusalem under the Persian governor's district, yet these men still came to help. Their labor reached toward the official seat or residence used by the governor when visiting the city.

A goldsmith named Uzziel and a perfume maker named Hananiah rebuilt the wall up to the Broad Wall. These men were skilled craftsmen rather than builders, yet they gladly did hard physical labor for God's city. The Broad Wall was an especially thick section that had survived earlier attacks without needing complete rebuilding.

Rephaiah, a leader over half the district of Jerusalem, repaired the next portion. Beside him, Jedaiah repaired the part directly across from his own home, followed by Hattush. Working on the wall right next to one's own house gave families a personal interest in making their section strong.

Malchijah and Hasshub repaired another section along with the Tower of the Ovens. This tower likely stood near public baking ovens or brick kilns along the wall. These men took on a difficult section that included both a wall and a defensive tower.

Shallum, who ruled the other half of the Jerusalem district, repaired the next stretch with the help of his daughters. His daughters may have paid for the building materials or helped supervise the workmen. God values and remembers the active support of women in doing His work.

Hanun and the residents of Zanoah repaired the Valley Gate, setting up its doors, locks, and crossbars. They also fixed about a thousand cubits of wall, or roughly fifteen hundred feet, reaching to the Dung Gate. This unusually long stretch was likely less broken down, allowing them to repair it more quickly.

Malchijah son of Rechab, ruler of the Beth-haccerem district, completely rebuilt the Dung Gate. He hung its doors and fastened its bolts and bars. This gate on the south side of the city was where waste and refuse were carried out to keep Jerusalem clean.

Shallun, ruler of the Mizpah district, rebuilt the Fountain Gate, covered it with a roof, and installed its doors and locks. He also rebuilt the wall around the Pool of Siloam near the royal gardens, reaching the stairs that led down from the City of David. This gate protected access to vital water supplies for the city.

A different leader named Nehemiah, ruler of half the district of Beth-zur, repaired the wall past the royal burial places of David's family. His section ran past a man-made water reservoir and the barracks known as the House of the Mighty. This area covered steep, rocky ground on the southern side of the city.

Levites under Rehum repaired the next section, followed by Hashabiah and Binnui, who each governed half of the Keilah district. The Levites, who normally took care of temple duties, readily shared in the city's defense. The two leaders of Keilah divided the work so that both parts of their home territory contributed fairly.

Ezer, a local ruler of Mizpah, repaired another section of the wall facing the path up to the armory at a corner bend. The armory was the city arsenal where shields and spears were stored for defense. Ezer made sure this strategically important corner received proper protection.

Baruch repaired the next section, from the corner turn to the doorway of the high priest's house, with great zeal. The writer notes his earnestness, showing that he threw himself into the labor with special energy and devotion. A single worker's passionate commitment can encourage everyone nearby to work harder.

Meremoth repaired a second section of the wall along the entire length of the high priest's house. Because he had already finished an earlier section near the Fish Gate, taking on this extra piece showed his generous spirit. God is pleased when His people go beyond what is required to help others.

Priests who lived in the surrounding plains, likely the Jordan valley near Jericho, repaired the next stretch of wall. Even though they lived in villages outside the city, they traveled to Jerusalem to help their fellow priests. Serving God often means leaving personal comfort behind to support the wider community.

Benjamin and Hasshub repaired the wall right in front of their home, while Azariah repaired the section beside his own house. Placing residents near their own dwellings ensured they would build solidly to keep their own families safe. Caring for the needs closest to our own doors is often the first step in serving God.

Binnui repaired another section to the corner, and Palal repaired opposite the projecting royal watchtower by the prison courtyard. Pedaiah then continued the repairs from that point. This section guarded the king's palace grounds and the high watchtower that kept guard over the city.

The temple servants, who did practical work around the sanctuary, lived on the hill of Ophel and worked opposite the Water Gate. This gate on the east opened toward the water springs and was near the great tower that jutted out from the wall. Working near their own quarters, these humble servants helped protect the entrance they used every day.

The men of Tekoa stepped forward to repair a second section of wall, reaching from opposite the great tower to the wall of Ophel. Even though their wealthy nobles had refused to do any work at all, the ordinary citizens gladly volunteered for double duty. God honors willing hearts that do extra work to make up for the failings of others.

Priests repaired the wall above the Horse Gate, each working directly across from his own residence. This gate stood near the temple and palace, where horses were led out to the valley or brought to stables. Having priests live and work side by side along the wall created a strong line of dedicated defenders.

Zadok repaired the wall opposite his house, while Shemaiah, the gatekeeper of the temple's East Gate, repaired the next stretch. Even though Shemaiah had official charge of a sacred gate, he pitched in on the city wall wherever help was needed. Faithful servants of God are willing to do whatever work needs doing, even beyond their regular title.

Hananiah and Hanun, the sixth son of his father, repaired another section, while Meshullam repaired opposite his single room. Hanun did not let being a younger son keep him from taking the lead in doing good. Meshullam's care for the wall opposite his small room shows that God notices what we do with whatever little space we have.

Malchijah the goldsmith repaired up to the building used by temple servants and merchants opposite the Inspection Gate, and other goldsmiths and merchants closed the gap back to the Sheep Gate. These tradesmen and sellers used their hands to close the final opening in the defenses. By finishing where the building first began, the workers brought the entire protective circle around Jerusalem to completion.
